content: Dr. Xavier Bosch-Capblanch, a group leader at the Swiss Tropical and Public Health Institute (Swiss TPH), can be contacted for further information. Meike Zuske from Swiss TPH coordinated contributors, while reviewers included Ekpereonne Esu and Chioma Moses Oringanje from the University of Calabar, who focused on effectiveness and safety reviews, and Heather Ames from Swiss TPH, who conducted a feasibility scoping review. Peter Steinmann, a lymphatic filariasis expert from Swiss TPH, contributed to the project, along with Amanda Ross and Dr. Bosch-Capblanch, who performed statistical analyses. John Eyers from Swiss TPH served as the search strategist. Special thanks are extended to Jonathan King from WHO for coordinating the review process with WHO guidelines and facilitating discussions among various groups. Mohammed T. Ansari reviewed the GRADE evidence profiles, and Gary Weil, Joshua Bogus, and Charles Goss from Washington University in St. Louis provided data from ongoing studies and responded to requests. The global elimination of lymphatic filariasis (LF) as a public health problem was targeted for 2020. However, as of now, 29 out of 55 countries requiring mass drug administration (MDA) are not on track to meet this goal. Some countries are only beginning to scale up MDA efforts, which require a minimum of five years to implement effectively. Many governments and donors have committed resources only through 2020, and further commitments remain uncertain. Countries initiating MDA programs are seeking advice from WHO on alternative strategies to accelerate progress and potentially stop MDA by the target elimination date. Additionally, countries that are on track are requesting guidance on addressing suboptimal responses to current MDA strategies, such as districts with persistent infection rates despite more than five annual MDA rounds, districts failing transmission assessment surveys (TAS) despite meeting eligibility criteria, and hotspots of infection identified during post-MDA surveillance. WHO is expected to recommend strategies to overcome these challenges and must respond promptly to national program queries by grading available evidence and establishing recommendations that consider the feasibility and accessibility of alternative strategies. Alternative MDA strategies, such as twice-yearly treatment with ivermectin (IVER), have been identified as potentially more effective in reducing infection and transmission in less time compared to the current five annual MDA rounds. Mathematical models support the effectiveness of twice-yearly treatment, and pharmacokinetic studies of a three-drug combination (IVER, diethylcarbamazine citrate [DEC], and albendazole [ALB]) have shown superior parasite-killing effects without increased serious adverse events, even in individuals with heavy parasite loads. This approach could potentially lead to permanent sterilization or destruction of adult worms, reducing infection and transmission below elimination thresholds more quickly than current strategies. Randomized clinical trials of this three-drug strategy have been initiated in five countries, with safety data available for meta-analysis. However, the use of DEC in countries co-endemic with onchocerciasis or loiasis is not recommended, and twice-yearly treatment with the current two-drug regimen may serve as an alternative in such settings. To provide the WHO guideline development group with the best available evidence, the Swiss TPH conducted an updated systematic review on the effectiveness and safety of mass chemotherapy for LF. This report includes the methods and results of the systematic review, as well as a feasibility scoping review of qualitative evidence on community perceptions of MDA regimens. The systematic review considered comparative studies with randomized allocation of drug interventions, including individualand community-level studies. Participants included individuals infected with or communities endemic for Wuchereria bancrofti or Brugia species. The review assessed alternative MDA strategies compared to the current strategy, focusing on outcomes such as microfilaria clearance, microfilarial density, circulating filarial antigen levels, and adverse events. The review identified nine relevant studies conducted between 2010 and 2017 in African, Asian, and Latin American countries. Most studies were randomized controlled trials (RCTs), with sample sizes ranging from 12 to over 10,000 participants. The studies primarily focused on adult participants, with some including children aged five years and older. Risk of bias (ROB) was assessed using standard criteria, and the quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Findings from the systematic review suggest that alternative MDA strategies, such as the three-drug combination, are more effective in achieving microfilaria clearance and reducing microfilarial density compared to the current two-drug regimen. However, the evidence is limited by the small number of studies and variability in study designs. The qualitative scoping review explored community and drug distributor perceptions of MDA campaigns for LF elimination. It included studies from countries undertaking MDA campaigns and focused on themes such as community acceptance, challenges in drug distribution, and the experiences of health workers and volunteers. In conclusion, the findings highlight the potential of alternative MDA strategies to accelerate LF elimination while addressing challenges in implementation and community acceptance. Further research and evidence synthesis are needed to refine recommendations and support national programs in achieving elimination goals.
